title: Your reading
tomorrow: give quietly, or give where people can see? Amira can't decide.

cards: A voice note to a friend, deleted and re-recorded four times because one word came out wrong. Reading aloud does that. Now make it a language you're still learning, and make it the Qur'an.
Is the stumbling a problem? Here's the odd detail. A hadith doesn't just tolerate the reader who stumbles.
It promises that reader two rewards.

teach.b: The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said the one who is skilled in the Qur'an will be with the noble, righteous scribes, the angels.
And the one who reads it haltingly, finding it hard, has two rewards. Why two? Commentators such as al-Nawawi give a plain reading: one for the reciting, and one for the effort it costs.
The stumble isn't held against the reader. It's counted. The Qur'an makes room for limits too.
Surah al-Muzzammil opens with a call to stand much of the night in prayer. Its last verse eases that call.
God knows, it says, that some of you are sick, some are traveling in search of His bounty, some are fighting in His cause.
So recite of it what is easy. That's the solution to the puzzle, and the idea behind a daily portion. Not the whole book in a weekend.
A set amount, sized to your actual life, kept every day: a page, a few verses, a short surah.
Some read slowly beside an audio reciter; some read a translation alongside. One for tonight: in the hadith, the struggling reader is promised two rewards.

how: Some Muslims read a set portion of the Qur'an each day, following its traditional divisions or a few verses at a time, sometimes reading the Arabic slowly with a recording or a teacher.

o: reading the whole Qur'an in one long sitting
listening to recitation instead of reading it
a daily Qur'an portion sized to your real life

p: one for reciting, one for effort

s: stumbling over Qur'an recitation cancels its reward
the hadith promises the one who finds it hard two rewards.
surah al-Muzzammil eases its own call to long night prayer
its last verse names the sick, the traveler and the fighter: recite what is easy.

games.q: your cousin decides to read the whole Qur'an this month. by day four she's behind and wants to quit. she asks you. what fits today?
o: catch up with one big all-nighter, then keep the pace.
set a smaller daily portion she can keep, and keep it.
quit for now and try again when she has more time.
games.why: 73:20 says recite what is easy, and the hadith counts the effort itself. a kept portion beats a dropped goal.

practice: Open a Qur'an or a translation, on paper or a screen, to any page. Choose one verse and stay with it for the whole sit: read it once, slowly, in whatever language you can, then rest your eyes on the words.

wordCard.voice: Your reading: a daily Qur'an portion sized to your real life, stumbles and all.
